items.followUp: What happens to an enzyme’s active site when the enzyme is denatured?

rubric.why: Identifies a factor that alters the enzyme’s structure.
rubric.description: Names a cause of denaturation.
rubric.how: Award for a valid cause such as high temperature or extreme pH.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of denaturation on enzyme function.
rubric.description: States that the altered enzyme loses its activity.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the change in structure or active site prevents the enzyme from working.

modelAnswer: High temperature, an extreme pH, or certain chemicals can change an enzyme’s three-dimensional structure.
The active site changes shape, so the enzyme can no longer catalyse its reaction.

items.followUp: Name two types of stains that enzymes in biological detergents can remove.

rubric.why: Identifies the use of proteases in removing protein-based stains.
rubric.description: Names an enzyme or its protein-stain target.
rubric.how: Award for proteases or an appropriate protein stain such as blood.

rubric.why: Identifies another enzyme and the stain it helps remove.
rubric.description: Names another enzyme or its stain target.
rubric.how: Award for lipases removing fats or grease, or amylases removing starch.

modelAnswer: Proteases in biological detergents break down protein stains such as blood.
Lipases break down fat and grease stains.

items.followUp: Name four cellular activities that require energy from ATP.

rubric.why: Recognises a cellular activity powered by ATP.
rubric.description: Names one ATP-requiring cellular function.
rubric.how: Award for any one valid function, such as biosynthesis, active transport, movement, or cell division.

rubric.why: Recognises another cellular activity powered by ATP.
rubric.description: Names a second ATP-requiring cellular function.
rubric.how: Award for a valid function distinct from the one credited in the first point.

modelAnswer: ATP provides energy for the synthesis of molecules and for active transport across membranes.
It also provides energy for muscle contraction and cell division.

items.followUp: What is the main energy-storing product of cellular respiration?

rubric.why: Identifies that respiration involves the breakdown of food molecules.
rubric.description: States that food, especially glucose, is broken down.
rubric.how: Award for describing the breakdown or oxidation of glucose or another food molecule in cells.

rubric.why: Identifies the energy outcome of cellular respiration.
rubric.description: States that energy is released and made available to the cell.
rubric.how: Award for stating that energy is released, particularly when stored in ATP.

modelAnswer: Cellular respiration is the process in which cells break down food molecules, especially glucose.
Energy is released and captured in ATP for the cell’s activities.

items.followUp: Where does glycolysis occur, and what are its main products from one glucose molecule?

rubric.why: Identifies the cellular location of glycolysis.
rubric.description: States where glycolysis takes place.
rubric.how: Award for cytoplasm or cytosol.

rubric.why: Describes the main breakdown product and energy yield of glycolysis.
rubric.description: States that glucose forms two pyruvate molecules with a net gain of two ATP.
rubric.how: Award for the two pyruvate products and net yield of 2 ATP.

modelAnswer: Glycolysis is a series of reactions in the cytoplasm in which one glucose molecule is broken down.
It forms two molecules of pyruvic acid and gives a net gain of two ATP molecules.

items.followUp: In the translocation of sugars in a plant, what is an example of a source and of a sink?

rubric.why: Defines the source as the plant part supplying food.
rubric.description: Defines or gives an example of a source.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a source produces or supplies sugars, such as a mature leaf.

rubric.why: Defines the sink as a plant part that uses or stores transported food.
rubric.description: Defines or gives an example of a sink.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a sink uses or stores sugars, such as a root, fruit, or growing region.

modelAnswer: A source is a plant part, usually a mature leaf, that produces and supplies sugars.
A sink is a plant part that uses or stores sugars, such as a root, fruit, or growing region.

items.followUp: Define Zoology and Botany, and name the third major division of Biology.

rubric.why: Gives the basic meaning of Biology.
rubric.description: Defines Biology.
rubric.how: Award for describing Biology as the study or science of life or living organisms.

rubric.why: Correctly describes Botany.
rubric.description: Names and explains the study of plants.
rubric.how: Award for identifying Botany as the study of plants.

rubric.why: Correctly describes Zoology.
rubric.description: Names and explains the study of animals.
rubric.how: Award for identifying Zoology as the study of animals.

rubric.why: Names and explains the third major division.
rubric.description: Names and explains Microbiology.
rubric.how: Award for identifying Microbiology as the study of microorganisms.

modelAnswer: Biology is the science of life and the study of living organisms.
Botany is the study of plants.
Zoology is the study of animals.
Microbiology is the study of microorganisms.

items.followUp: Define enzymes and describe one use of an enzyme in the food industry and one in detergents.

rubric.why: States the defining catalytic role of enzymes.
rubric.description: Defines enzymes as biological catalysts.
rubric.how: Award for identifying enzymes as biological catalysts that speed up reactions without being used up.

rubric.why: Gives a valid industrial application of enzymes.
rubric.description: Names an enzyme use in food processing or detergents.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example, such as rennin in cheese-making or proteases in detergents.

rubric.why: Provides a specific enzyme application or another industrial sector.
rubric.description: Adds a relevant example of enzyme use in industry.
rubric.how: Award for a correct enzyme and target, or a valid industrial application such as textile, leather, or paper processing.

rubric.why: Shows how enzymes are applied to an industrial process or material.
rubric.description: Explains the effect or purpose of an industrial enzyme use.
rubric.how: Award for stating what the enzyme does in the named process, such as breaking down stains or aiding cheese-making.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions without being used up.
In the food industry, rennin is used to coagulate milk during cheese-making.
Proteases in detergents break down protein stains, while lipases break down fats and grease.
Enzymes are also used in textile, leather, and paper processing.
